What this tool is — and is not

  • This tool produces an indicative planning estimate only — it is not a quotation, a guarantee of savings, or an assessment of your eligibility for any government program.
  • Every number below is a modelled assumption shown to you in full. Your actual outcome depends on your retailer and tariff, your metering and export limits, the size and orientation of the installed system, how you use power, and the weather.
  • Government incentive programs, their eligibility rules and their value change over time. Always confirm current program conditions with the official source and with your installer before making a decision.

How the model thinks

Six things worth understanding about your own numbers

The model is deliberately simple so the reasoning stays visible. These are the steps it takes — and the assumptions that limit it.

Your bill becomes consumption

The model divides your quarterly bill by an assumed usage rate to estimate annual kWh. Supply charges are excluded, because solar cannot reduce them. If you know the rate you actually pay, use the override — it sharpens every figure downstream.

Consumption becomes an array size

Generation target = consumption (× 1.0, or × 1.1 when a battery can absorb the surplus), divided by your region's yield and adjusted by the roof factor. Shade and orientation are represented by that factor — a blunt instrument standing in for a roof assessment.

Generation splits three ways

Direct self-use first, set by the daytime profile; surplus to the battery, limited by usable capacity, efficiency and realistic cycling; everything left is exported at the feed-in rate. Self-consumed kilowatt hours avoid the retail price — far more valuable than exports.

Battery value comes from your evening peak

A battery is worth the electricity it displaces. If your household imports little in the evening, storage has less to save — no matter how large the capacity. The comparison table above shows both sides of that question rather than asserting an answer.

It models a year, not a season

The maths uses annual averages, so it cannot show a cloudy June or a scorching January. Seasonal swings are real and expected; a single bad month is weather, not a failed model. Annual figures are what a system is sized against.

Uncertainty lives in the range

The ±20% band reflects weather, prices and behaviour — three things no model can predict for you. Treat the numbers as planning tools with visible assumptions, not as commitments.

An estimate is a model. A proposal is an assessment.

No honest provider can guarantee savings, payback or incentive eligibility, because all three depend on weather, market prices, program rules and how the household uses power. What a provider can commit to is the specification, the compliance work and the price. Treat every savings figure on this site — and in any quote — as an assumption audit: check what went in, and what could change.

Turn the estimate into an actual design.

The estimate uses averages. A proposal uses your interval data, your roof and your tariff — and states the assumptions it relies on.
